title: Word Ladder
description:
Word Ladder

A transformation sequence from word beginWord to word endWord using a dictionary wordList is a sequence of words beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk such that:

  • Every adjacent pair of words differs by a single letter.
  • Every si for 1 <= i <= k is in wordList. Note that beginWord does not need to be in wordList.
  • sk == endWord

Given two words, beginWord and endWord, and a dictionary wordList, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, or 0 if no such sequence exists.

Examples:

  • Input: beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"]
    Output: 5
    Explanation: One shortest transformation sequence is "hit" -> "hot" -> "dot" -> "dog" -> cog", which is 5 words long.
  • Input: beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log"]
    Output: 0
    Explanation: The endWord "cog" is not in wordList, therefore there is no valid transformation sequence.

Constraints:

  • 1 <= beginWord.length <= 10
  • endWord.length == beginWord.length
  • 1 <= wordList.length <= 5000
  • wordList[i].length == beginWord.length
  • beginWord, endWord, and wordList[i] consist of lowercase English letters.
  • beginWord != endWord
  • All the words in wordList are unique.
solution_text:
Search by Distance with Breadth-First Search

Think of each word as a node in a graph. Two words are connected when they differ by exactly one letter. The problem asks for the shortest path from beginWord to endWord, which is exactly what breadth-first search (BFS) finds in an unweighted graph.

The BFS queue stores a word and the number of words used to reach it. The starting entry is (beginWord, 1) because the sequence already contains the beginning word.

  1. Put every dictionary word in a set for fast lookup. If endWord is absent, return 0 immediately.
  2. Remove a word from the set as soon as it enters the queue. This marks it as visited and prevents cycles or repeated work.
  3. Take the next word from the queue. If it is endWord, return its distance.
  4. Generate neighbors by replacing each character position with each lowercase letter. Add valid, unvisited dictionary words to the queue with distance plus one.
  5. If the queue becomes empty, no transformation exists, so return 0.

Why this works: BFS explores all sequences of length 1 before length 2, all of length 2 before length 3, and so on. Therefore, the first time it reaches endWord, that sequence must be the shortest.

Complexity: Let N be the number of words and L their length. Each visited word tries 26 · L changes, and constructing a changed string costs O(L), for O(N · L2) time when the alphabet size is treated as constant. The set and queue use O(N · L) space.
